idiom_name: PropertyChangeSupport + PropertyChangeListener (all properties or one by name)
implementation_notes: PropertyChangeSupport implements the whole role structure for bound properties: add/removePropertyChangeListener (for all properties or one by name), firePropertyChange(name, old, new), hasListeners, and the class is documented as thread-safe. It replaces the classic java.util.Observable/Observer pair, which is deprecated since Java 9 and should not be used in new code. PropertyChangeListener is a functional interface, so a lambda works as an observer, but the listener must be held in a variable to be removable.
pitfalls: firePropertyChange(name, old, new) suppresses the notification when the values are equal; a listener that must observe every assignment needs the event-object overload or a different signal.
Listeners are strongly referenced - the classic Swing leak: a component that registers and never removes stays reachable, so removal belongs in the same lifecycle method as registration.
Notification is synchronous on the calling thread: a listener mutating UI state must re-dispatch to the EDT, and a listener that throws aborts the remaining listeners.
Registering the same listener twice delivers two notifications; the API does not deduplicate.

variants.name: java.util.concurrent.Flow (reactive-streams, JDK 9)
variants.implementation_notes: The JDK 9 Flow API is the flow-controlled realization: SubmissionPublisher implements Flow.Publisher and delivers submitted items to each subscriber asynchronously through an Executor, while Flow.Subscriber receives a Subscription whose request(n) provides backpressure and whose cancel() unsubscribes. It replaces the synchronous listener loop with an asynchronous, ordered, cancellable pipeline and corresponds to the reactive-streams specification. Choose it when item volume or subscriber count is high or when slow consumers must not block the publisher; PropertyChangeSupport remains the simpler choice for local synchronous updates.
pitfalls: Subscriber methods run on the publisher's executor: blocking inside onNext starves the other subscribers and must be avoided or moved to another executor.
Backpressure is manual - forget request(n), or request one item without renewing, and the stream stalls silently instead of buffering for you.
Cancellation is cooperative and terminal: after cancel() no onComplete/onError is sent, and calling request() afterwards is a no-op.
SubmissionPublisher does not apply flow control of its own beyond the buffer size given to the constructor; an oversized or tiny buffer changes drop/stall behaviour.
